en: Laziness is the cause of a man's insignificance, the destroyer of both dharma and worldly prosperity, a lack of vigor in one's being, a humiliation of oneself, and the extinguisher of human status;
it is touched by those of mediocre qualities, adopted by the base, and abandoned by the best of men.
By which Brahmins fall away from tranquility, as if due to some external omen:
the failure to obtain what has not been gained, the certain loss of what has already been obtained, self-contempt, and the humiliation by those who are superior. (15.1.4)
From indolence comes the loss of luster, the cessation of learning, discipline, and contentment for men, and they fall into ruin. (Saundarananda 16.95)
Having heard this method, he is unable to attain further growth;
having known the supreme Dharma, he is unable to dwell upon it;
and having abandoned his home and become liberated, he is unable to attain peace.
In this matter, indolence is the cause for a man; it is not his enemy. One who seeks the highest good must certainly not be without exertion.
With hearts attached to indolence and consisting of pleasure,
Aśvaka and Punarvasuka, having succumbed to indolence, fell into hell even after seeing the Buddha. (15.1.7)
If laziness did not exist as a calamity in the world, by what means would anyone here become wealthy or highly learned?
It is through indolence that this earth, extending to the edge of the oceans, remains so.
It was filled with human cattle who were destitute;
[yet it belonged] to one who was indifferent toward his own body, skillful, and resolute.
For one who has initiated vigor according to the right method, nothing is difficult to accomplish. A man attains the fruit of his labor through efforts such as plowing and the like;
by walking, he traverses the path, whereas by not walking, he does not go.

That they have attained liberation and that they are established in heaven—exertion is the cause in both cases; therefore, one should be devoted to vigor. Since the highest good is achieved through effort, and not from a Lord nor by chance.
Who would flee from cyclic existence, which is like a burning house?
Therefore, considering vigor to be supreme, he whose own vigor and prowess were firm—the best among speakers—said, "O Ānanda, vigor is for the sake of awakening. (15.3.4–5)
Fire is born from wood when it is rubbed; the earth yields water when it is dug.
For men who possess perseverance, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.
All efforts undertaken according to the right method bear fruit.
Fire arises from wood through friction,
and the earth indeed yields water when it is dug.
Even one who travels very slowly reaches the end of the road;
what then can a man not accomplish here if he exerts his vigor?
For vigor is not attained in this world without effort.
Success is not attained even by a man of superior intelligence; therefore, those who desire to achieve supreme success must apply themselves with diligence, possessing both wisdom and vigor. 15.3.8
For those men who possess zeal, vigor, and heedfulness, all prosperities rest in the palm of their hands;
therefore, these are the causes of all success.
A wise person desiring constant success should devote themselves [to this],
placing their foot upon the head of sleep and pleasure, and likewise upon the head of the enemy of laziness and the base.
The pair of feet of those who have initiated valor with undiminished courage is served by Fortune;
nothing whatsoever is difficult for them through their prowess.
Therefore, with unflagging persistence,
strive for the goal;
for those who are constantly active indeed succeed in due time.
Even a stream of water [softens] a surface of stone.
Therefore, you who desire great prosperity, being firm-minded and ever-vigilant, exert yourselves with true vigor.
For by means of vigor, humans attain Buddhahood—the benefactor of the three worlds—which is worthy of worship by the lords of gods, humans, and asuras. (15.3.12)
